pulls.title: decouple accounturi validation from challenge object
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Builds on #30 by @slghtr-says. Rebased onto main with additional changes by @sheurich.

### Summary

PR #30 added `accounturi` to the challenge object. The changes here address a coupling issue: #30 defined `accounturi` validation in terms of the challenge object, but the challenge object does not exist in the JIT validation path or when records are pre-provisioned.

### Changes

**Decouple `accounturi` validation from the challenge object.** The DNS record requirement (§4 item 3) now stands on its own: the `accounturi` MUST be a URI identifying the requesting ACME account, and the CA MUST verify it. No reference to the challenge object. Works for JIT, pre-provisioned, and standard challenge flows.

**Many-to-one `accounturi` model.** CAs MUST accept the ACME account URL (RFC 8555 §7.3). CAs MAY also accept alternative URIs, provided each uniquely and permanently identifies a single account (RFC 8657 §5.4). Non-reassignment and deactivation lifecycle requirements included. This addresses the privacy concern raised by @birgelee — publicly visible `accounturi` values in long-lived DNS records create a correlation channel (RFC 8657 §5.9). See the new Account URI Privacy subsection in Security Considerations.

**`accounturi` in the challenge object remains required.** The field is the mechanism by which the CA communicates the expected URI (including alternative URIs) to the client.

**Add `accounturi` comparison semantics.** Simple String Comparison per RFC 3986 §6.2.1. PR #36 adds a consolidated comparison paragraph for all parameter values; the inline rule here serves as a standalone fallback.

**Add pre-provisioning guidance (new §4.4).** How to construct records without a challenge object: use the ACME account URL from the `Location` header, obtain `issuer-domain-name` from `caaIdentities` as a hint (not normatively coupled). Operational guidance: maintain record inventory, use `persistUntil`, audit after DNS incidents. CAs SHOULD maintain stable account URIs and document their guarantees.

**Add JIT rate-limiting and abuse guidance.** Per-domain rate limiting independent of requesting account. CAs SHOULD restrict JIT to accounts with prior successful `dns-persist-01` validation (trust-on-first-use). Account activity logging for the JIT path.

**Fix DNSSEC failure semantics.** Resolved a SHOULD/MUST inconsistency: DNSSEC validation remains SHOULD, but if a CA performs it, failure MUST be treated as a challenge failure. Includes rationale for the stricter-than-RFC-8555 requirement.

**Fix DNS caching caveat.** Revocation section previously said "after the record is removed, new validation attempts will fail" — misleading. Now says "after the record is removed and resolver caches have expired."

**Neutralize §4 example prose.** Changed "it might provision" to "the DNS TXT record would contain" — removes assumption that the client provisions after receiving the challenge. Add `accounturi` to §Examples challenge objects for consistency.

**Error handling.** Changed "does not match the URI" to "does not identify the ACME account" — covers both account URL comparison and alternative URI resolution.

**Terminology.** Use "URI" consistently (matching the parameter name and RFC 8657), "ACME account URL" only for the RFC 8555 §7.3 concept.

comments.author: sheurich
comments.body:
@slghtr-says @birgelee — This PR builds on Michael's #30 with changes from my review. Here's what I changed and why.

### The main fix

PR #30 defined DNS record validation in terms of the challenge object ("MUST match the `accounturi` provided by the CA in the challenge object"). This breaks for JIT validation (no challenge object exists) and pre-provisioned records. The DNS record requirement now stands on its own — the `accounturi` MUST be the ACME account URL, verified by the CA against the requesting account. The challenge object provides the same value for client convenience.

### Other changes

**Removed "any other URI as determined by the CA."** This conflicts with RFC 8657 §3, which defines `accounturi` specifically as the ACME account URL. If future use cases (EAB, sub-accounts) need alternative identifiers, they'll need normative definition in a separate section. @slghtr-says — this touches on the flexibility discussion from your earlier conversation with @birgelee. I think the right path is to handle those use cases explicitly if and when they materialize, rather than an open-ended escape hatch.

**Added comparison semantics.** Simple string comparison per RFC 3986 §6.2.1, matching RFC 8657's own comparison rule. No normalization, no percent-decoding.

**New pre-provisioning section.** Documents how to construct records without a challenge object — account URL from the `Location` header, `issuer-domain-name` from `caaIdentities` (as a hint, not normatively coupled). Operational guidance on record inventory, `persistUntil`, post-incident audit.

**JIT hardening.** Per-domain rate limiting (not just per-account), trust-on-first-use for JIT eligibility, account activity logging.

**DNSSEC fix.** The draft says DNSSEC validation "SHOULD" be performed. Adding an unconditional MUST-on-failure created a contradiction. Now conditional: if a CA validates DNSSEC, failure MUST be treated as a challenge failure.

**Account URL stability.** CAs SHOULD maintain stable account URLs and document their guarantees. If they must change URL structure, they SHOULD provide a transition period.

comments.body:
So my high level thoughts on this is I like the better support for JIT and pre-provisioned records. Both of these are things to lean into.

I don't really like forcing the accounturi to be the one-to-one mapping with the ACME account. I think it should be many-to-one so subscribers validating multiple domains with the same ACME account and hide that these domains share the same ACME account (today there is no way of deducing this so we are introducing a new information channel to adversaries).

Maybe we could just add a clause saying you MUST accept the "URI of the ACME account object" but you MAY also accept other "URI values such that each URI uniquely identifies a single ACME account in perpetuity". I think this would support both sides because a user could still pre-provision records using only their true ACME account URI but they could also use a system put in place by the CA to obfuscate ACME account bindings.

comments.body:
> So my high level thoughts on this is I like the better support for JIT and pre-provisioned records. Both of these are things to lean into.
>
> I don't really like forcing the accounturi to be the one-to-one mapping with the ACME account. I think it should be many-to-one [...]
>
> Maybe we could just add a clause saying you MUST accept the "URI of the ACME account object" but you MAY also accept other "URI values such that each URI uniquely identifies a single ACME account in perpetuity".

Agreed with this framing. The revision implements what you describe: MUST accept the URI of the ACME account object, MAY accept other URIs where each uniquely identifies a single ACME account permanently. Normative constraints (non-reassignment, deactivation invalidation, RFC 8657 §5.4 uniqueness) bound the flexibility that PR #30's original language lacked.

This also aligns with how BR 3.2.2.4.22 references RFC 8657 — only §3 is normatively relevant, and §3 permits the many-to-one model. Section 5.3's multi-system consistency requirement is about CAA processing, not dns-persist-01 validation.

I have some serious concerns with tight coupling this to the Account URI using a 1-to-1 mapping. Right now, with the exception of RFC8657 users (which is a very small percentage of domains) there is no way from public logs to correlate two domains back to the same ACME account. Being able to do so opens up tons of infrastructure discovery avenues as two domains using the same ACME account indicates with high probability those domains are hosted on the same server/hosting infrastructure. Then, if there is a vulnerability in the software stack at one domain, it could be used to compromise the other domain.

I am hoping to have this method see widespread adoption and I think if it leaks ACME account bindings it could hinder adoption.

Nothing in Michael Slaughter's CAB/F ballot forces this type of coupling. I have already spoken with several CA owners about plans to either using hashing or a back-end database maintained by the CA to issue virtual URIs for the purpose of DCV.

I think the main security parameter needed for this uri is that there exists some function F known to the CA such that F(URI) -> exactly 1 ACME account in perpetuity.  There can be multiple URIs that produce the same ACME account.

Additionally a small change: I am not aware of any definition of acme account URL in RFC8657. Should "the ACME account URL of the account" be changed to "ACME account URI"?

I also, I know it was in the original draft, but I don't super love RFC8657 as a reference since it is not the ACME RFC itself and RFC8657 is generic to ACME and non-ACME while this I-D is ACME specific. I feel like this is a bit of an indirect reference. Sec 3.1 of RFC 8657 defines "URI of the ACME account object" when making the proposal ACME specific.

comments.body:
The `accounturi` field description says it is “the sole mechanism by which the CA communicates the expected value to the client”, but this isn’t true for the pre-provisioning / JIT paths described later (where there is no challenge object). Consider scoping this statement to the normal challenge flow (e.g., “when a challenge object is used…”) or rephrasing to avoid implying that challenges are always available.
```suggestion
- **accounturi** (required, string): A URI identifying the ACME account requesting validation, as defined in {{!RFC8657}}, Section 3. This is the URI the CA expects in the DNS record; when a challenge object is used, this field communicates the expected value to the client. Clients that pre-provisioned a record using their ACME account URL ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3) SHOULD verify the value identifies the same account.
```

Item 3 states “Comparison rules for `accounturi` values are specified below”, but there is no subsequent section defining those comparison rules (and the document doesn’t reference RFC 3986). Either add the promised comparison semantics section or remove/adjust this sentence to avoid leaving implementers without a deterministic comparison algorithm.
```suggestion
    CAs MUST accept the URI of the ACME account object ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3) as a valid `accounturi` value. CAs MAY also accept other URIs, provided each such URI uniquely and permanently identifies a single ACME account and satisfies the uniqueness requirements of {{!RFC8657}}, Section 5.4. CAs MUST NOT reassign a URI to a different account. When an ACME account is deactivated, CAs MUST treat all URIs associated with that account as invalid for validation purposes. The CA MUST verify that the URI in the DNS record identifies the ACME account making the request. Comparison of `accounturi` values MUST follow the URI comparison rules in {{!RFC3986}}, Section 6.
```

This paragraph still allows non-account-URL identifiers ("CAs MAY also accept other URIs"), which conflicts with the PR description’s “Pin `accounturi` to ACME account URL” / removal of alternative URIs. Please align the spec text with the intended behavior (either remove the alternative-URI allowance, or update the PR description and any related text to reflect that alternatives remain supported).

The pre-provisioning guidance requires using the ACME account URL from the `Location` header, but earlier item 3 allows CAs to accept alternative `accounturi` values. If alternatives are supported, this section likely needs to describe how a domain owner can obtain/provision those alternative URIs without a challenge object, or clarify that pre-provisioning is limited to the ACME account URL form.
```suggestion
- **accounturi**: The ACME account URL, as returned in the `Location` header of the account creation response ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3). This specification defines pre-provisioning only for this ACME account URL form. If a CA wishes to support alternative `accounturi` formats for use in pre-provisioned records, it MUST provide a mechanism, described in its documentation, for domain owners to obtain those alternative values without requiring a prior challenge object; such mechanisms are out of scope for this document.
- **issuer-domain-name**: Clients MAY use the `caaIdentities` array from the ACME directory metadata ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 9.7.6) as a hint for `issuer-domain-name` selection. CAs that populate `caaIdentities` SHOULD ensure these values are consistent with the `issuer-domain-name` values they accept in `dns-persist-01` records. If `caaIdentities` is unavailable, the `issuer-domain-name` MAY be obtained from the CA's Certificate Policy or Certification Practice Statement.

Organizations pre-provisioning records SHOULD maintain an inventory of `_validation-persist` records and the ACME accounts they reference. Records SHOULD include a `persistUntil` parameter to bound their effective lifetime. Domain owners SHOULD audit `_validation-persist` records after any DNS infrastructure security incident, as pre-provisioned records persist beyond the window of compromise.

CAs implementing `dns-persist-01` SHOULD maintain stable account URIs used in `dns-persist-01` records, including the ACME account URL form used for pre-provisioning, for the lifetime of the account and SHOULD document their URI stability guarantees. If a CA must change its URI structure, it SHOULD provide a transition period during which both old and new URIs are accepted for validation.
```

The last sentence suggests clients who pre-provisioned using their ACME account URL “SHOULD verify the value identifies the same account,” but if the CA uses an alternative `accounturi` scheme (allowed later), a client generally can’t determine whether an arbitrary URI maps to its account without an explicit CA-provided linkage. Consider clarifying how a client can perform this check (or weakening/removing the SHOULD in cases where the CA’s `accounturi` is not the account-object URL).
```suggestion
- **accounturi** (required, string): A URI identifying the ACME account requesting validation, as defined in {{!RFC8657}}, Section 3. This is the URI the CA expects in the DNS record; it is the sole mechanism by which the CA communicates the expected value to the client. Clients that pre-provisioned a record using their ACME account URL ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3) SHOULD verify that the `accounturi` value exactly matches that URL. If the CA uses a different form of `accounturi` that is not the account-object URL, the client is not expected to determine equivalence and MUST rely on the `accounturi` value provided by the CA.
```

Agreed on all three. Here's how I addressed them:

**Many-to-one mapping:** My concern with PR #30's "any other URI as
determined by the CA" was the absence of constraints, not the
flexibility itself. Your formulation (F(URI) → exactly 1 account)
provides the right bound, and RFC 8657 §5.9 makes the privacy
motivation concrete for dns-persist-01's long-lived public records.

Revised item 3: CAs MUST accept the URI of the ACME account object
(RFC 8555 §7.3) as baseline. CAs MAY also accept other URIs, provided
each uniquely and permanently identifies a single account (citing
RFC 8657 §5.4 for uniqueness). CAs MUST NOT reassign URIs, and
deactivated accounts' URIs MUST be treated as invalid. This preserves
pre-provisioning (clients use their account URL when no challenge
object exists) while letting CAs offer per-domain virtual URIs. The
challenge object's `accounturi` field becomes the delivery mechanism —
stated explicitly as the sole mechanism by which the CA communicates
the expected value.

I also revised the SHOULD-verify text in the challenge object
description — clients can't match against their account URL when the
CA provides a virtual URI.

**Terminology:** Using "URI" in normative text and "ACME account URL"
only when referring specifically to the RFC 8555 §7.3 concept.

**Reference:** Keeping RFC 8657 §3 as the normative reference for
accounturi semantics in the challenge object definition. Item 3 cites
RFC 8555 §7.3 for the account URL and RFC 8657 §5.4 for uniqueness.
Dropped the §3 citation from the MAY clause to avoid tension with §3's
language.

I added an Account URI Privacy subsection to Security Considerations
covering the correlation risk, opacity and mapping integrity
requirements, CP/CPS disclosure, and the auditability trade-off.

One coordination note: PR #36 consolidates comparison semantics for
all parameter values (accounturi, policy, persistUntil) in a single
paragraph after item 5. I trimmed the comparison sentence from item 3
here to avoid redundancy — item 3 ends with a forward reference to
the comparison rules below.
Fixed in db1efc9 — dropped "sole mechanism," now reads "the mechanism by which the CA communicates alternative URIs to the client."

Fixed in db1efc9 — replaced the dangling forward reference with an inline rule: "In the absence of more specific comparison rules, implementations MUST use Simple String Comparison as defined in RFC 3986, Section 6.2.1." PR #36 adds the consolidated comparison paragraph that elaborates; this inline rule is a standalone fallback that works regardless of merge order.

PR description updated. The many-to-one model is intentional — see the discussion thread with @birgelee above. The original "Pin accounturi to ACME account URL" language was from the first iteration; the spec was revised to MUST accept the account URL, MAY accept alternatives with constraints.

The asymmetry is intentional. Pre-provisioning happens before any challenge object exists, so the only URI the client has is the account URL from the `Location` header. Alternative URIs require the CA to generate and deliver them via the challenge object. No change needed — §4.4 already scopes itself to "When constructing records without a challenge object."

The SHOULD is scoped to clients that pre-provisioned using their account URL, so when the CA returns that same URL, they can string-compare. The question is what happens when the CA returns a virtual URI instead — the client cannot verify equivalence independently.

Two options:

**(a)** Leave as-is. SHOULD already permits not verifying when you cannot (RFC 2119). A client that receives a URI different from their account URL knows they did not pre-provision with it and moves on.

**(b)** Make explicit:

```
Clients that pre-provisioned a record using their ACME account URL
(RFC 8555, §7.3) SHOULD verify the value matches that URL; if the
CA provides a different URI, the client SHOULD use the CA-provided
value for subsequent DNS record updates.
```

This tells implementers what to do in both cases without over-specifying.

@birgelee @slghtr-says — preference?

> Records SHOULD include a `persistUntil` parameter to bound their effective lifetime. 

Why? Can you explain how you see this being used? For out of band provisioning it would be possible to automate persistUntil update out of band, to update it in a loop constantly, but it seems very useless as it is an automation of an unnecessary work. If organizations maintain inventory of DNS records like mentioned (for example if they use IoC tools for setting DNS), then DNS records / account keys can just be tracked and removed. 

Or maybe you meant MAY here instead of SHOULD?

Changed to MAY in 4b735dc. The parameter is already MAY in the record format (item 5), so SHOULD here was inconsistent. Organizations managing record lifecycle through IaC or inventory tooling don't need a second expiration mechanism. The persistUntil considerations section (§8.3) already covers operational guidance for those who do use it.

Validation Record Format item 2 requires the `issuer-domain-name` to match one of the `issuer-domain-names` values from the challenge object. That coupling conflicts with the later "Pre-Provisioning Records" and JIT paths, which explicitly operate without a challenge object. Consider redefining this requirement in terms of the issuer-domain-names the CA accepts/configures for dns-persist-01 validation, and treat the challenge object's `issuer-domain-names` array as just the mechanism to convey those acceptable values when a challenge object is used.
```suggestion
2.  The `issuer-domain-name` portion of the issue-value MUST be one of the Issuer Domain Names that the CA accepts for `dns-persist-01` validation. When a challenge object is used, the CA-conﬁgured acceptable Issuer Domain Names MUST be conveyed in the `issuer-domain-names` array of the challenge object. If the `issuer-domain-name` does not match any of the values accepted by the CA, the CA MUST reject the record.
```

The Verification Procedure currently states that `issuer-domain-name` MUST match one of the values from the challenge object's `issuer-domain-names` array. This is incompatible with the Just-in-Time validation flow described later (where no challenge object is returned) and with pre-provisioned records. It would be clearer to specify matching against the CA's accepted issuer-domain-names for the validation attempt, with the challenge object's array being one way of communicating those accepted values.
```suggestion
The ACME server verifies the challenge by performing a DNS lookup for TXT records at the Authorization Domain Name. It then iterates through the returned records to find one that conforms to the required structure. For a record to be considered valid, its `issuer-domain-name` value MUST match one of the issuer-domain-names that the CA accepts for the current validation attempt (for example, values communicated via the challenge object's `issuer-domain-names` array, if a challenge object is used), and it MUST contain an `accounturi` parameter that identifies the requesting account. When comparing issuer domain names, the server MUST adhere to the normalization rules specified in {{challenge-object}}. The server also interprets any `policy` parameter values according to this specification. If no record meeting all requirements is found, the server MUST treat the challenge as failed.
```

The note explaining the `policy` case-insensitivity requirement says that without it "some CAs might reject unknown parameter values". But the surrounding normative text already requires treating any `policy` value other than `wildcard` as if the parameter were absent, so implementations should not reject unknown `policy` values. Consider rewording this note to focus on the actual risk (e.g., rejecting otherwise-valid `policy=wildcard` due to case differences) to avoid implying that unknown values should be rejected.
```suggestion
    Note: The requirement to ignore unrecognized parameters (item 1) ensures forward compatibility, allowing future extensions without breaking existing implementations, consistent with ACME's extensibility model ({{!RFC8555}}). The explicit case-insensitivity requirement is necessary to ensure consistent behavior across implementations; without it, some CAs might reject otherwise-valid `policy=wildcard` values or handle them inconsistently when the tag or value casing differs (e.g., `PoLiCy=WiLdCaRd`), undermining interoperability and protocol evolution.
```

comments.body:
hot take, is persistUntil actually a good idea? I know its in the ballot (browsers like it) but it does have a chance of shooting people in the foot. I guess including it as a SHOULD statement is not a huge deal one way or the other, but my personal operational advise if a sysadmin asked me would be to not use it unless you put in a system designed to automate the updating of the persistUntil record. Such a system would need DNS credentials and we would be back at square one. Maybe this is just my overly operationally-minded opinion, but CNAME records never had a persist until value...

sort of fine going either way on this, but wanted to put it out there.

During the discussion period of SC-088v2, a concern was raised about the complexity that relying on the TTL of the DNS TXT record for validation reuse period consideration would introduce. https://groups.google.com/a/groups.cabforum.org/g/servercert-wg/c/QWUbL8VRx2o/m/DdMVzgJ9AAAJ

Ultimately, this led to SC-088v3 removing the TTL consideration and instead fixing the validation data reuse period to 10 days regardless of the TTL.

For additional context, this was discussed when ``persistUntil`` was originally added to SC-088. https://github.com/slghtr-says/servercert/pull/3/changes/BASE..b588937f8512c9cb972b65b1d4472f841da0ec0b#r2167738350

This was the rationale: 

> A distant expiry date, set without robust automation and monitoring, could lead to unexpected certificate issuance failures when the deadline is reached and no action has been taken. While the risk is real, it feels manageable and, arguably, a necessary trade-off for the optional ability to terminate a delegation. The ability to signal termination seems like a fundamental security control, especially given the potential for delegations to be forgotten or misused. Making this optional for the Applicant seems to offer a reasonable approach to risk management for all parties involved. This also aligns with the principle of least privilege and shares a similar characteristic with SC-085, where a Applicant has performed a security function and we intend to honor it.

I agree that the mechanism introduces a foot-gun but ultimately I agree that there are legitimate use cases where the persistUntil mechanism enhances the security of the DCV method. 

Perhaps we should add a note (or another sentence to this note) that speaks to the danger of a domain own setting a persistUntil value for a domain intended to renew to some date "far" in the future without sufficient automation or monitoring around it.
See comment here: https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/pull/35#discussion_r2890907684

I'm strongly in favor of dropping persistUntil. It makes sense and is easy to support from the server side. But it is actually a _total pain_ to support from the client side (as we have discovered in the process of implementing dns-persist-01 in multiple ACME clients).

If you're a site operator and you're using persistUntil, there are three possible outcomes:
1) You don't have automation to detect when it's about to expire, and validation breaks. This is bad.
2) You do have automation to detect when it's about to expire, but don't have automation to update the record. This is repeated manual effort. This is bad, and preventing this was the whole point of ACME.
3) You do have automation to detect when it's about to expire, and you have automation to update the record. This is just dns-01.

None of these outcomes is, in my opinion, sufficiently valuable to justify the extra complexity. I wish it hadn't made it into the ballot, and I'd love it if we could remove it from this spec.
I share similar concerns about the TTL, and filed this bug about it just yesterday: https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/issues/42

Yes, very much agree, I found persistUntil extremely weird, so just didn't implement it, and don't see implementing it until the use case is found, it is like DNS-01 but slightly different and not even better. Supporting it in the client requires all of the complexity of DNS-01 and more. While it is interesting that it is possible to signal termination in other way, other than just removing the record, I can't see any use case where it is required.

> You do have automation to detect when it's about to expire, and you have automation to update the record. This is just dns-01.

For what @aarongable mentioned here^ one point to see is that unlike DNS-01 it is trivial to decouple DNS record automation from ACME client. 
Like it is possible indeed to increment persistUntil date of the record in a loop somewhere on another machine even, only while the client that needs it is running... But... why?
At the same time it is also easy to do the same by health monitoring and removing the record too.

Actually you can pretty much implement persistUntil in user space by just monitoring the records, parsing persistUntil, and then actually removing the records if they are expired, ACME server doesn't even have to support them.

For temporary short-lived resources maybe persistUntil could be used, but again seems like an extra complexity for something that isn't really needed and will be a foot gun.

The security model of automating DNS-PERSIST-01 in the same way as DNS-01 is automated currently is slightly worse, as DNS-01 token is unique for each challenge but here it is possible to issue multiple certs using the same DNS record while it is valid, while still requiring write access to the DNS records. persistUntil only seems to make sense if there is some external and possibly complex orchestration for automating extension of the record lifetimes, but even then it benefits seem marginal.

I'm not too strongly against it, as it is optional on the client side, but IMO for those cases where it could be used DNS-01 should be used instead, or some custom logic layer on top of the dns persist records could be written, it seems like a part of the spec that is destined to rot as no one will use it.

pulls.title: Clarify case-handling rules for parameter values
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Addresses #34.

## Problem

The draft requires case-insensitive comparison for `policy` values but says nothing about the case-handling of `accounturi` or `persistUntil` values. An implementer (@beautifulentropy, working on [Pebble support](https://github.com/letsencrypt/pebble/pull/536)) asked: what makes `policy` special?

The asymmetry is correct, but the draft doesn't explain it:
- `accounturi` values are URIs — case-sensitive per RFC 3986
- `persistUntil` values are integers — case is inapplicable
- `policy` values are protocol keywords — case-insensitivity is a deliberate usability choice

RFC 8659 §4.1 makes parameter *tags* case-insensitive but defines no rules for parameter *values*, leaving that to whichever specification defines the parameter.

## Changes

**Item 4 (policy parameter):** Replace the ambiguous sentence *"The parameter's 'tag' and its defined values MUST be treated as case-insensitive"* with a statement scoped to `policy` values only. The tag clause was redundant (already covered by RFC 8659 §4.1).

**New paragraph after item 5:** State the case-handling rules for all parameter values in one place:
- `accounturi`: Simple String Comparison per RFC 3986 §6.2.1; MUST NOT case-fold
- `policy`: case-insensitive (protocol keywords, often manually provisioned)
- `persistUntil`: base-10 integer; case does not apply

## Compatibility with #35

PR #35 adds `accounturi` comparison semantics to item 3 (simple string comparison, no normalization/case-folding). The new paragraph here reinforces that without conflicting. Both PRs can merge in either order.

comments.body: Item 4 now defines case-insensitive comparison for `policy` values, but the later rule "if its value is anything other than `wildcard`" (outside this hunk) could be misread as only matching the lowercase literal. Consider explicitly tying that later check to this case-insensitive comparison rule (e.g., by saying the comparison to `wildcard` is case-insensitive per item 4).

The note following item 4 appears to justify forward compatibility by saying some CAs might reject unknown *parameters*, but item 4 is now about case-insensitive comparison of `policy` *values* (and unknown-tag handling is already covered in item 1). Consider updating this note to refer to unknown `policy` values (or moving/removing it) so the rationale matches the requirement being stated.
```suggestion
    Note: This requirement ensures consistent, interoperable handling of the `policy` parameter. By requiring case-insensitive comparison of `policy` values, future extensions (for example, additional policy names) can be introduced without risking mismatches between clients and CAs that differ only in the letter case they use, consistent with ACME's extensibility model (RFC 8555, Section 7.3).
```

This is the only place in the document that uses the normative subject "Implementations MUST". Elsewhere requirements are scoped to specific actors (e.g., "CAs MUST", "Clients MUST"). For clarity and conformance testing, consider scoping this requirement explicitly (e.g., what CAs MUST do when verifying `accounturi`, and whether any requirements apply to clients).
```suggestion
- `accounturi`: The value is a URI. When verifying a `dns-persist-01` challenge, CAs MUST compare `accounturi` values using Simple String Comparison per {{!RFC3986}}, Section 6.2.1, with no case-folding or other normalization.
```

This Note predates this PR — it explains the forward-compatibility requirement in item 1 ("the server MUST ignore any parameter within the issue-value that has an unrecognized tag"), not the case-insensitivity rule in item 4. The Note is about unknown parameter *tags* being ignored; item 4 is about known parameter *values* being compared case-insensitively. Different requirements, different scopes. Leaving as-is.
Good catch — scoped to "CAs MUST compare" since the comparison happens server-side during challenge verification. Clients write the value; CAs verify it.

The fallback clauses ("if its value is anything other than `wildcard`") define semantics — what happens when `policy` is not `wildcard` — not comparison mechanics. The comparison operation is governed by item 4's unconditional MUST: "Comparison of the values defined for this parameter MUST be case-insensitive." That rule applies to all comparisons of `policy` values, including these fallback checks.

The fallback clause at line 180 is 8 lines below item 4's case rule and its worked example (`"WILDCARD" and "wildcard" are equivalent`). §5 and §6 both cross-reference §4 via `{{wildcard-certificate-validation}}`. An implementer who reads item 4 (which they must, to understand `policy`) will see the case rule before reaching the fallback.

Adding parenthetical cross-references to each fallback clause would conflate semantic definitions with comparison mechanics, and create 3 additional maintenance points for a rule already normatively defined in one place. Leaving as-is per IETF convention: define once, reference forward.

pulls.title: fix(terminology): rename "Authorization Domain Name" to "Validation Domain Name"
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Closes #40

## Problem

The draft defines "Authorization Domain Name" as the full DNS label where the validation TXT record is provisioned (e.g., `_validation-persist.example.com`). The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements define the same term as the bare FQDN used to obtain authorization (e.g., `example.com`). This conflict causes implementer confusion — especially once issue #33 adds an `adn` (Authorization Domain Name) field that uses the BR definition.

## Change

Rename the draft's concept to **"Validation Domain Name"** — aligning with RFC 8555 Section 8.4, which uses "validation domain name" for the analogous `_acme-challenge.<FQDN>` label in the dns-01 challenge. All 10 occurrences across 9 locations are updated:

| Section | Context |
|---|---|
| §2 Conventions | Glossary heading + definition body |
| §3 Challenge | Overview paragraph |
| §4 Challenge Response | Provisioning instructions (×2), example, server verification |
| §4.1 Multiple Issuer | CA verification step 1 |
| §4.3 JIT Validation | DNS lookup target |
| §6.8 Revocation | Record removal instructions |
| §8.2 Wildcard Example | Record provisioning step |

The glossary definition cites both the RFC 8555 precedent and the BR disambiguation.

## What this does NOT change

- No normative behavior changes — pure terminology rename
- No changes to record format, validation procedure, or security properties

## Prerequisite for

- **Issue #33** (subdomain validation prompting) — the `adn` field uses "Authorization Domain Name" in the BR sense; this rename clears the way

comments.body:
RFC 8555 doesn't define a term for this concept, but it does call it a "validation domain name" in one sentence (emphasis added):

> The record provisioned to the DNS contains the base64url encoding of
> this digest.  The client constructs the **validation domain name** by
> prepending the label "_acme-challenge" to the domain name being

pulls.title: fix: DNSSEC SHOULD needs deviation consequence (RFC 2119)
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Closes #44

The bare SHOULD in §9.6.1 had two problems:

1. **No RFC 2119 deviation consequence.** BCP 14 requires SHOULD to indicate what happens when the requirement is not met. The old text gave no guidance.
2. **Wrong verb.** "Validate DNSSEC signatures" describes implementation behavior; the actual requirement is resolver choice — use a DNSSEC-validating resolver.

### Changes

```diff
- To ensure the integrity of the validation process, CAs SHOULD validate
- DNSSEC signatures on `dns-persist-01` TXT records.
+ CAs SHOULD use a DNSSEC-validating resolver when querying
+ `dns-persist-01` TXT records. Without one, a CA will silently accept
+ forged responses in DNSSEC-signed zones.
```

The conditional MUST for fail-closed behavior is unchanged:

> If a CA performs DNSSEC validation, it MUST treat validation failure [...] as a challenge failure and MUST NOT use the record for domain validation.

### Context

- Raised during IETF 124 ACME WG session
- #1: resolved not to mandate DNSSEC deployment
- #17: moved DNSSEC from normative requirements to security considerations
- #28: simplified to bare SHOULD (created the gap)
- SC-085 (cabforum/servercert#579): requires DNSSEC-validating resolver for WebPKI CAs

comments.body:
The statement "Without one, a CA will silently accept forged responses" is phrased as an absolute outcome. In practice, the risk is that the CA cannot *detect* forged/spoofed answers (and may accept them) when DNSSEC is not validated, rather than forged responses always being present. Consider rewording to reflect inability to detect/mitigate forged responses (e.g., "may accept" / "cannot detect") to avoid overclaiming.
```suggestion
DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) {{?RFC4033}} provide cryptographic authentication of DNS data, ensuring that the validation records retrieved by a CA are authentic and have not been tampered with. CAs SHOULD use a DNSSEC-validating resolver when querying `dns-persist-01` TXT records. Without one, a CA cannot detect forged or spoofed responses in DNSSEC-signed zones and may silently accept them. If a CA performs DNSSEC validation, it MUST treat validation failure (e.g., expired signatures, broken chain of trust) as a challenge failure and MUST NOT use the record for domain validation. This requirement is stricter than the general DNSSEC guidance in {{!RFC8555}} because `dns-persist-01` records are long-lived and their compromise would persist for the record's lifetime.
```

After switching the SHOULD to "use a DNSSEC-validating resolver", the following MUST still refers to when "a CA performs DNSSEC validation". To avoid ambiguity about whether relying on a validating resolver counts, consider explicitly tying the MUST to that mechanism (e.g., "If a CA performs DNSSEC validation (including via a DNSSEC-validating resolver)...") so implementers know the fail-closed requirement applies in that case too.

pulls.title: feat: support subscriber-account URIs in `accounturi`
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Fixes #57. Closes #55. Closes #54.

## Summary

Allow `accounturi` in dns-persist-01 records to identify a CA subscriber account encompassing multiple ACME accounts. See #57 for the problem statement, RFC 8657 basis, design rationale, and security analysis.

## Changes

### §2: Subscriber Account definition

Defines "Subscriber Account" as a "CA account" (RFC 8657 §3) that encompasses one or more ACME accounts. Maps the term to the normative reference and explains the naming choice (disambiguation from ACME accounts, which are also CA accounts).

### §4.1 item 3: three-mode structure

| Mode                        | Cardinality | Comparison                                | Requirement |
|-----------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------|
| (3a) ACME account URL       | 1:1         | Simple String Comparison                  | MUST accept |
| (3b) Alternative URI        | many:1      | Simple String Comparison or CA resolution | MAY accept  |
| (3c) Subscriber-account URI | 1:many      | CA-internal lookup                        | MAY accept  |

Constraints on 3c:
1. CA MUST verify the requesting ACME account is associated with the subscriber account
2. CA MUST document the URI format and association model in CP/CPS
3. Non-reassignment and deactivation lifecycle requirements carry over
4. CA MUST log which specific ACME account was used for each subscriber-URI validation
5. CA SHOULD make subscriber URIs syntactically distinguishable from per-account URIs

Resolves #55: the trust model is now unambiguous for each URI type. Clients can independently verify 3a (string comparison), may be able to verify 3b (if the CA exposes the mapping), and cannot verify 3c (must trust the CA).

### §6.8: revocation rewrite

| Action                        | 3a (ACME URL)          | 3b (Alt URI)           | 3c (Subscriber)             |
|-------------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Remove DNS record             | ✓ (after cache expiry) | ✓ (after cache expiry) | ✓ (after cache expiry)      |
| Deactivate ACME account       | ✓ (immediate)          | ✓ (immediate)          | ✗ (only that account)       |
| Deactivate subscriber account | N/A                    | N/A                    | ✓ (immediate, all accounts) |

CAs supporting subscriber-account URIs MUST provide a subscriber-account deactivation mechanism.

### §7.2: account binding security

- Existing claim that security is "fundamentally bound to the security of the ACME account's private key" is incomplete for subscriber URIs — bound to any key under the subscriber plus the subscriber account management system.
- New subsection (§7.2.1) on subscriber credential compromise: compromise of the CA's account management system lets an attacker add ACME accounts that immediately inherit all persistent authorizations.

### Security considerations

Addresses all nine interactions from #57:
- Interactions 1–3 and 6–8: new subsections or additions in Security Considerations
- Interaction 4: addressed by §6.8 rewrite
- Interaction 5: addressed by §4.1 restructure
- Interaction 9: addressed by new §7.2.1 subsection

### Other text updates

- §1: qualify "uniquely identifies the applicant's account" to cover subscriber accounts
- §3.1: broaden `accounturi` field description; add per-mode client verification guidance
- §4.4: subscriber URI as pre-provisioning source; forward-authorization advisory
- Case-handling rules: Simple String Comparison for 3a/3b; CA-internal verification for 3c
- Error handling (§9.3.1): cover the subscriber-association failure mode
- §7.6 CAA interaction: use `dns-persist-01` consistently; note CAA and dns-persist `accounturi` as independent reinforcing checks
- Quote RFC 8657 §3 "group of related entities" directly in normative text

## Deferred

- Client mismatch behavior (#59) — warrants focused treatment per mode
- IANA error type registration (#39) — new failure mode noted but not registered
- `adn` response field (#33) — forward-referenced only
- Naming conventions (#56) — independent editorial issue
- TTL validation reuse (#42) — independent issue

No new JSON fields, DNS record syntax, or IANA registrations. The change is purely semantic.


In mode 3c, saying “deactivating a single … ACME account only removes that specific account from the subscriber relationship” is a CA-internal detail that may not be true (the relationship could persist while the ACME account is simply unusable/deactivated). Consider rephrasing to the externally observable effect: deactivating that ACME account prevents it from using the subscriber-level authorization, but does not affect other associated ACME accounts or invalidate the subscriber-level record.
```suggestion
2. **Deactivate ACME account:** For situations requiring immediate revocation of issuance capability (e.g., suspected account key compromise), an ACME account can be deactivated as specified in {{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3.6. For modes 3a (ACME URL) and 3b (Alternative 1:1 URI), this serves as a full emergency measure, effectively invalidating the record's utility. For mode 3c (Subscriber-account URI), deactivating a single compromised ACME account prevents that ACME account from using the subscriber-level authorization, but does NOT affect other associated ACME accounts or invalidate the subscriber-level record.
```

The client guidance says clients that pre-provisioned using their ACME account URL “SHOULD verify the value identifies the same account”, but it doesn’t specify what the client is expected to do if verification fails (e.g., abort the order, warn the operator, or treat it as potential mis-issuance). Consider adding an explicit behavior on mismatch to make the SHOULD actionable and interoperable.
```suggestion
- **accounturi** (required, string): A URI identifying the specific ACME account requesting validation or a subscriber account encompassing it (see {{validation-record-format}}), using the identifier format specified in {{!RFC8657}}, Section 3. This is the URI the CA expects in the DNS record and the mechanism by which the CA communicates alternative URIs to the client. Clients that pre-provisioned a record using their ACME account URL ({{!RFC8555}}, Section 7.3) SHOULD verify the value identifies the same account. If the client can independently verify the value and determines that it identifies a different account, the client MUST NOT rely on the pre-provisioned record for that challenge and SHOULD treat the mismatch as a misconfiguration or potential unauthorized issuance attempt and alert the operator. Note that independent verification is possible for mode 3a (Simple String Comparison), may be possible for mode 3b (if the CA exposes the URI-to-account mapping), and is not possible for mode 3c (clients must trust the CA's subscriber-account association).
```

In the Validation Record Format requirements, item 3 still says the `accounturi` value “identifies the ACME account requesting validation”, but mode 3c allows `accounturi` to identify a subscriber account that *encompasses* the requesting ACME account. This is internally inconsistent and could be read as forbidding mode 3c. Consider updating item 3’s lead-in sentence to cover all three modes (direct ACME account identification for 3a/3b, subscriber-account identification plus association check for 3c).

Constraint 5 (“CA SHOULD make subscriber-account URIs syntactically distinguishable…”) introduces a normative SHOULD without stating what the expected consequence/risk is if a CA does not do this, and “syntactically distinguishable” is underspecified (distinguishable by whom, and how). Consider either making this non-normative guidance, or specifying concrete, testable criteria (e.g., a dedicated URI scheme/prefix) and why it matters (e.g., auditability, avoiding confusion with 1:1 comparison semantics).
```suggestion
        5.  Subscriber-account URIs are best made syntactically distinguishable from per-account URIs, for example by using a dedicated URI scheme or a stable path prefix documented in the CP/CPS. Doing so improves auditability and reduces confusion with 1:1 per-account URI handling, where comparison semantics may differ.
```

Valid gap. The SHOULD verify clause predates this PR but adding the per-mode verification note makes the gap more visible. Mismatch behavior interacts differently across modes: for 3a, string mismatch is definitive; for 3b, it depends on whether the client can resolve the mapping; for 3c, the client cannot verify at all. That complexity warrants focused treatment rather than a sentence grafted onto this change.
Tracked in https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/issues/59

reviews.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
reviews.body:
## Pull request overview

Copilot reviewed 1 out of 1 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments.

comments.body: The PR introduces the term “subscriber account” / “Subscriber-account URI” but the document doesn’t define what a “subscriber account” is or how it relates to RFC 8657’s defined term “CA account” (“a specific entity or group of related entities”). Per the draft’s account-identity guidance, consider either (a) using the RFC 8657 term consistently (e.g., “CA account” / “CA-account URI”), or (b) adding a definition in Conventions and Definitions that explicitly maps “subscriber account” to the RFC 8657 concept to avoid ambiguity for implementers and auditors.

In the CAA interaction note, the inline identifier ``dns-persist`` isn’t used elsewhere in the draft (the challenge type/label is consistently “dns-persist-01”). This is likely to confuse readers about whether the statement refers to the ACME challenge, the IANA label, or something else—please use the same identifier here as in the rest of the document (or explicitly define what ``dns-persist`` denotes).
```suggestion
The `dns-persist-01` validation method is a valid `validationmethods` parameter value for CAA records per {{!RFC8657}}. Note that CAA `accounturi` and `dns-persist-01` `accounturi` are independent reinforcing checks — both can restrict issuance, and subscriber URIs in one do not automatically apply to the other.
```

reviews.author: birgelee
reviews.body: I like it, would just remove the "1:1" reference to avoid confusion.

comments.body:
I think we are on the same page with what this method is in tended imply, but I wonder if using "1:1" will confuse people. I would expect a 1:1 to mean that there is exactly 1 alternative URI mapping back to an ACME account and there can exist no other alternative mapping strategies.

I understand the language is not intended to mean this (the next sentence specifically says "URIs" implying there can be multiple mappings), but I had always thought of this as a many-to-one not 1:1 style mapping.

We could also just drop the "1:1" reference together and just call this something like "Alternative URI**"
This would imply that CAs that support HTTP reverse proxies (which is currently allowed) would accept arbitrary URI origins.
Why does the ACME key need to be compromised for this attack? Surely the attacker could legitimately create their own ACME account.

I don't follow. The account URI in the record doesn't have to actually be usable for real (like have a web server able to respond to it). It's just an arbitrary string that should map to an account from the CA's perspective.
The issue is that a CA operating under mode 3a would be prohibited from requiring that the URI uniquely identifies the account.

Perhaps this is more relevant for commercial providers where it's not as easy to create an attacker controlled account? But even if the attacker can spoof DNS responses with a victim's Subscriber-account URI, the attacker still needs to have compromised one of the victim's account keys in order to sign the ACME requests with, right?
Wait what? 3a is already how ACME CAs operate today where accounts have a single URI value that uniquely identifies the account. Why would they be prohibited from continuing to do that?

The issue is that an RFC8555 account URI doesn't uniquely identify the account and CAs like Let's Encrypt allow the domain name in an account URI to be changed while still referring to the same account. This can cause a security issue with this challenge type as a valid account URI might point to an attacker controlled domain.

Sure it does. An account URI today only refers to a single account on the CA side. If the CA changes (for example) the domain in the account URI, the new URI still only refers to a single account on the CA side. You just now have two account URIs that uniquely identify an account (assuming the CA still recognizes the old one).

Perhaps we're interpreting the phrase "uniquely identify the account" differently? I take it to mean that at any given time, an account URI can refer to only one account on the CA side. There can theoretically be many account URI values that refer to the same account. But they can all only refer to a single account.

on this point I will mention that this is the existing behavior inherited from RFC 8657 which shares many of these same security considerations. Additionally, if we assume the CA and the subscriber are benign, it seems unlikely the subscriber will intentionally put in an arbitrary adversary-controlled prefix to their accounturi. A goal for this standard is to maintain consistency with RFC 8657, so I am somewhat keep this language as is.

The context for this is imagine a CA which has some type of non-ACME subscriber relationship (e.g., an enterprise account) which contains multiple ACME accounts within it (say an ACME account for each ACME client within the enterprise). These associated ACME accounts are understood by the CA and only the enterprise administrator can make new ACME accounts within the enterprise.

CAB/F participants have asked to let this method support specifying the account URI of the **enterprise subscriber** account and permit this to authorize issuance by the sub ACME accounts. One security consideration of this approach is that it creates a larger attack surface because there are now N different authorized ACME accounts and a compromise of the private key of any one of those accounts will authorize issuance. IMO the alternative of forcing a single ACME account for the entire enterprise will just mean the same ACME private key will be spread over N different servers, so I think this is a good approach to facilitate enterprise use cases.

My understanding of this text is that its introduced to help explain this security consideration. I will say I find the combination of DNS record spoofing and this enterprise account attack surface expansion somewhat confusing as if the attacker is capable of spoofing a DNS record, the obvious attack is to just spoof their own account URI in the record. My proposal would be to remove the words spoofing and focus the section on the expanded attack surface that comes from enterprise level subscriber accounts.

RFC 8657 only has a MAY requirement on accepting ACME account URIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8657#section-3.1-1) instead of the MUST requirement here.

I think what I've been trying to say is that given dns-persist-01's reliance on HTTPS, CAs should be given the option to reject some account URIs that they otherwise allow for other methods e.g. Let's Encrypt should be allowed to reject http://invalid.example/acme/acct/3285011975 as an account URI for the purposes of this method.

@MaxHearnden agreed, the MUST is stronger than warranted. We're revising mode 3a to SHOULD with a soft-redirect:

> (3a) ACME account URL: CAs SHOULD accept the URI of the ACME account object (RFC 8555, §7.3) as a valid `accounturi` value. A CA that does not accept the account URL directly MUST provide an alternative URI in the challenge `accounturi` field (mode 3b or 3c).

Reasons why this is the right level:

1. RFC 8657 §5.2 gives CAs explicit discretion over which parameters to recognize and how to interpret them. §5.3 goes further in that a CA that can't support the parameters uniformly MAY split into multiple CAA-processing identities, and one that can't even do that MUST NOT implement the parameters. A MUST on mode 3a overrides that design.

2. The challenge-response `accounturi` field (§3.1) already works as a substitution mechanism, as the CA can return a different URI than what the client proposed. A MUST on accepting the raw account URL makes that channel pointless for mode 3a. SHOULD preserves it.

The soft-redirect ensures subscribers always get a working `accounturi` regardless of which modes a given CA supports.

@birgelee the SHOULD preserves §5.2's variance model while the redirect keeps subscribers from hitting a dead end.

Agreed, the DNS-spoofing framing conflates two threats and makes the section harder to follow. The concern specific to §7.2.1 is attack surface expansion: N authorized ACME accounts under one subscriber relationship means N private keys that could lead to unauthorized issuance. DNS manipulation is orthogonal and already covered under MPIC.

The attacker doesn't need to compromise an existing key — they need access to the subscriber's account management system to add a new account. The current §7.2.1 text says this, but the parent section muddies it by leading with key compromise scenarios.

I'll revise §7.2 and §7.2.1:

1. Separate key compromise (§7.2 parent, all modes) from subscriber-management compromise (§7.2.1, mode 3c).
2. Drop DNS spoofing references — orthogonal, already addressed under MPIC.
3. Focus §7.2.1 on the enterprise attack surface expansion per @birgelee's proposal.

pulls.title: Add procedure for accounturi verification
pulls.author: MaxHearnden
pulls.body:
This PR adds a procedure for ACME clients to verify accounturis. The important step is to make a POST request to the accounturi endpoint, the token field/parameter is just so that ACME servers can force clients to implement the verification process.

This also requires the accounturi to be a valid ACME endpoint however I wasn't sure where it should be stated in the draft.

comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
My suggestion is that we should not overload the server with more requests that must be done.

A better solution would be as I have suggested, allow the client to compute the "accounturi" value offline by using a pubkey: "protocol" which is the sha256 value of the public key computed using the SPKI format over the account key - which also makes it crypto agility since the algoritm is included in the SPKI.

Meaning, a "TLSA" record calculator over the account public key would give the correct sha256 value.

Like:
_validation-persist.yourdomain.tld IN TXT "letsencrypt.org;accounturi=pubkey:fa759db3816ab7387006c8fb5b887a6fc3dde2d77f593ec2a8bf6504524da26e"

or use the JWK thumbprint.

By permitting a offline-calculation, all security considerations with a compromised accounturi is erased - at the cost of requiring record update if you choose to rotate account keys.

pulls.title: new mode to allow for public key.
pulls.author: sebastiannielsen
pulls.body: Closes https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/issues/64 if merged.

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body:
Hi all,

We are moving to decline this PR primarily on implementation grounds. We do want to move forward with a public-key hash mechanism, but we would like to take it in a slightly different direction. Internally we have aligned on the following format for hashing:

SHA-256(pubkey || accountURL || domain)

(|| for concatenation) This hash strategy has strong alignment with what is already required by the CA/Browser Forum and provides stronger security properties than pubkey alone.

Essentially, the justification for putting both the standard account URL and the pubkey in the hash is that the pub key provides sufficient entropy to avoid the account URL enumeration hashing attack (i.e., just iterating through account URLs until finding one that hashes to the observed value) while the account URL ensures CA/B Forum compliance and avoids complications with multiple accounts that share keys.

The current wording from the CA/B Forum reads "The `issue-value` MUST contain an `accounturi` parameter, where the parameter value is a unique URI (as described by RFC 8657, Section 3) identifying the account of the Applicant which requested validation for this FQDN; ". I feel that SHA-256(pubkey || accountURL || domain) satisfies this criteria because of the collision-resistant properties of hashes. There can only be one input that produces this hash so the hashed value can serve to uniquely identify the accountURL. SHA-256(pubkey) does not provide this same guarantee as two accounts could use the same key (potentially even between CAs). Obviously additional restrictions in the ecosystem like constraints on accounts reusing keys could be enforced, but I would argue that this comes at the cost of significantly more complexity (and could be a security risk, known bad keys could be tried during account registration to see if they are used by an ACME account).

In addition to stronger CA/B Forum language compliance, SHA-256(pubkey || accountURL || domain) solves the reused pubkey problem in a much more head on manner. Key reuse between accounts (or even accounts at different CAs) never risks overlaps in DCV.

Finally, we felt there are some advantages to keeping it in the URL format. Although the URI specifier can be much more broad, keeping it to a URL simplifies string comparison (its always byte-for-byte identical), and has nice multi-CA namespace isolation. Right now I am considering a scheme somewhat like:

https://<ca directory URL domain name>/.well-known/account-hash/<SHA-256(pubkey || accountURL || domain)>


Thank you again for this PR. I do think it is helping us move in the right direction by approaching these problems more head on, but we would prefer not to go with a special-purpose "pubkey" URI format.

comments.author: MaxHearnden
comments.body:
> Essentially, the justification for putting both the standard account URL and the pubkey in the hash is that the pub key provides sufficient entropy to avoid the account URL enumeration hashing attack (i.e., just iterating through account URLs until finding one that hashes to the observed value) while the account URL ensures CA/B Forum compliance and avoids complications with multiple accounts that share keys.

Just to restate my issue with the privacy claim.

As I had stated in https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/issues/61#issuecomment-4443182076, using SHA-256 as proposed still allows an attacker to determine if two domains were issued from the same account. Furthermore given knowledge of an account URI (maybe from a single CAA record or from brute forcing two domains) and a single SHA-256(pubkey || accountURL || domain) one can quickly (with a single hash operation) determine if that account is used for another domain.

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body:
@MaxHearnden am I correct in understanding that your attack is based on the assumption that the adversary knows the account URI or at least has a candidate account URI in mind that they want to test? I know you point out account URIs can be leaked via CAA record's accounturi parameter, but if the account URI is being leaked through this channel, I feel the adversary could perform the same infrastructure linkage through the CAA accounturi parameter.

I see the goal of this system I think of as mostly to prevent bulk infrastructure linkage through internet-wide scanning done through platforms like Shodan and Censys. If an adversary digs deep I feel shared infrastructure can usually be uncovered (it was discussed on list if this entire privacy system had a point because of this reason) and if a victim's account URI is leaked I feel that is out of scope for this mechanism.

I think even pairwise attacks (i.e., a function that can return True/False on two specific to tell if they use the same account URI) are sort of less of a concern as well. I think the only real risk comes from plaintext accountURIs as an adversary can just cheaply search for them in other places.

With that said, there is a potential approach of using an HMAC where the CA shares an HMAC key (say k) with the client (during new order or ideally account provisioning) and the client computes HMAC_k(pubkey || accountURL || domain). Collision resistance of hashes means that even if an adversary is between the CA and the ACME client, the adversary cannot construct a k' such that

HMAC_k(pubkey_adversary || accountURL_adversary || domain) = HMAC_k'(pubkey_victim || accountURL_victim || domain)

Since the adversary could never convince the victim to upload the HMAC to its account, this would still stop the MitM attack.

That said, this would hurt pre-provisioning unless it was communicated at account registration time which to me seems like an expensive lift for this system.

This would violate section 7.3.5 of RFC 8555 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555#section-7.3.5) which states that
```
   Note that changing the account key for an account SHOULD NOT have any
   other impact on the account.  For example, the server MUST NOT
   invalidate pending orders or authorization transactions based on a
   change of account key.
```

note "pending". Meaning that completed authorizations may be invalidated for security purposes.

The security risk of leaving a valid authorization, after a keyChange has been performed, is that two accounts may be authorized to issue for a single DNS record, which violates CAB/F rules that explicitly state that each DNS record may only reference a single CA account.

So a pending authorization would still be valid, since the challenge has not been completed. A completed authorization would however be invalidated, which can result in a pending order being invalidated - but that does not mean the order was invalidated as a consequence of a keyChange, but a dependent (completed) authorization.

The reason to invalidate a authorization is also that the security status of the account has been changed, which may warrant the CA changing the status of completed authorizations or challenges, as they are no longer valid for issuance at issuance-time.

The rationale of not invalidating pending transactions is to not break the state in a client and thus cause a desync in the client, where a client believes the pending authorizations are still valid, and try to complete them, even tough the server have changed state. **For authorization reuse, the client re-checks the state of authorizations, and would see the state change and update its local state, so the risk of invalidting a completed authorization is less of a risk - because a CA may invalidate a authorization for other purposes (mississuance, etc) so the client MUST recheck a authorization before reusing its status.**
Changed the pull to explicitly prohibit invalidating authorizations that have another state than "valid".
Why is this a MUST? CAs might decide that once a key has been used for an account, it can't be reused again for a different account.

I feel that a key should be able to be transferred between accounts at will of the subscriber. a CA should only blacklist a key if it believes the key has been compromised - OR if the key is already assigned to another account (ergo in use - 2 accounts may never share the same key ever at the same time).

Thats why I suggested the point 2 to avoid a CA falling into violation of the CAB/F rules by disallowing a authorization based on the old key to remain valid for issuance after the key has been moved to a new account.

There can be several reasons a subscriber wants to move a key to another account - for example if a subscriber sells his company but want to remain in control of other domains provisioned on the same key, - or an user leaving a web hotel where the web hotel manages the ACME accounts.

This doesn't prevent a CA from invalidating account keys that may be sensitive, or invalidating account keys as a result of a company going bankrupt. (to prevent computers and servers having the keys from being abused after they have been sold in a bankrupty auction).

**What the MUST says is that the keyChange action may never cause a key to be blacklisted in itself. If a subscriber intentionally want to blacklist a key, they should invalidate the account instead, which will invalidate the key aswell forever.**

This creates 2 distinct actions - either you keyChange to keep the old key usable, or you invalidate account if you want to also block the old key.

Theres little value in keeping the account itself, especially now when the new CAB/F rules that state that authorizations may only be valid for 7 hours when certificate validity goes down to 45 days.

_Another reason to wanting to go back to a old key, is if a key rollover fails spectacularly, and the subscriber want to roll back the key and retry again at a later time.
Blacklisting a key because it has been "used" would cause the subscriber to not be able to revert the key rollover if something goes south._

Of course this means, that keys that may leak after a rollover could still be usable - thats why its important that a subscriber removes any old previous DNS-PERSIST-01 pubkey: records after having completed a key rollover process and also have verified everything works with the new key.

pulls.title: Change language since issuer-domain-name is a opaque value
pulls.author: sebastiannielsen
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/issues/63 if merged

This because issuer-domain-name is just a opaque value, and "protecting" that value with DNSSEC - especially if its a legacy domain name that the CA does not own anymore, will not give any security advantage.

It would be analogous to protecting a sign outside a bank with heavy security but have glass doors to the vault.

The sensitive resource for a CA - that needs protecting - is the ACME Directory URL - also called Server URL. Thats the sensitive ACME resource the CA owns and is the root of trust for the ACME client.

comments.author: orangepizza
comments.body: doesn't CA/B rule require them to be included in CAAidentifer (from CCADB)?

comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
> doesn't CA/B rule require them to be included in CAAidentifer (from CCADB)?

Correct, but the value itself is opaque from client's point of view. Meaning, the client doesn't use the value in a particular way - it doesn't fetch a document from the domain, it doesn't verify the domain, it doesn't use the domain at all. 
so lets say letsencrypt would have CAAIdentifier = "letsencrypt.org, freecertificates.org"
and then letsencrypt loses control of freecertificates.org, maybe by losing the EPP transfer code to a malicious party.

That would not mean the security of the ACME protocol is compromised, since nobody uses the domain in the regular sense.
You could aswell have a number that identifies the CA in a public "CA list" or whatever:

```
example.com IN CAA 0 issue "534535;"
example.com IN CAA 0 issuewild "534535;"
```
and
`_validation-persist.example.com IN TXT "534535; accounturi=https://letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/58358493; policy=wildcard"`


The point im making is that the value itself doesn't have any meaning - its just a opaque string. It could be a sha256 hash of a public key or whatever. The value is only used in a string matching to the CAAIdentifier from CCADB.

MEANING: as long as the value exist in CPS and CCADB - its ok. The value itself doesn't need to be secured with DNSSEC. **The CA doesn't even need to own the value.**


The value is only used to capture intent of the domain owner. In the same way voting systems in different countries can be different, some have you write down the number of the president you want to vote on, some have you tick a box at the president's name, some have you write the name of the president, and some have you put pre-filled ballots for your president.

**Since the value doesn't have any meaning in itself, it doesn't matter if a third party owns the value. Even if a CA would call themselves "sebbe.eu" in CAAIdentifier, it would not matter. I would not gain something out of it.
Even if the record would look super weird with:**

`_validation-persist.example.com IN TXT "sebbe.eu; accounturi=http://someca.org/acme/acct/3950359; policy=wildcard"`

**I would still not be able to "compromise" the CA in any way. I would not be able to subvert their ACME traffic, I would not be able to issue for the domain, I would gain nada, zip from a CA "borrowing" my domain as their CAAIdentifier.**

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body:
Hi @sebastiannielsen ,

I see your point that there is no constraints on issuer domain name so recommending protection of it may be illogical.

My only thought on your change is is this paragraph needed at all? Recommending protection of ACME directory URL feels a bit like its just something that should have been brought up in the ACME standard.

Just curious if a flat out cut would be a better edit.

I am not particularly opinionated, just wanted to put this out there.

Best,
Henry

comments.author: MaxHearnden
comments.body:
It's important to note two things:
1. DNSSEC doesn't prevent DNS based denial of service, it just checks the authenticity of signed records. More records might be required for secure operation than just A/AAAA and without those additional records, an attack such as a BGP hijack might be effective even without spoofing any DNS records.
2. ACME as defined by RFC 8555, while is intended to be transported over HTTPS, is designed to be secure even when unencrypted. The example given for why this security is important is inside a CDN that connects to the backend servers over HTTP. At the moment, dns-persist-01 does rely on HTTPS and so additional security measures might be necessary for secure operation.

comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
@birgelee Yeah, a cut would work if https://github.com/ietf-wg-acme/draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist/pull/65 is implemented.
But then Pull #65 must be mandatory support.

Since #65 is optional support, I think the paragraph should be included - but correctly be referring to the ACME Server URI.

The security issue mentioned in the paragraph is only relevant for DNS-PERSIST-01 - since that relies on information solely from the ACME server. Not the ACME standard as a whole - since the other authentication methods rely on both a token AND client computed information (mandatory) - which means a malicious ACME server cannot in any way get a client to provision a valid record or file that would allow the malicious party to issue certificates for the domain.

@MaxHearnden 
The problem here is that while the other authentication methods specifically rely on client-computed information AND a token from the ACME server, the DNS-PERSIST-01 method ONLY relies on information from the ACME server. This is the security issue that the DNSSEC paragraph is intended to resolve - if the ACME Server (or its domain) is comrpomised, it means you could issue accounturi's that belongs to an attacker.

Note that even if the ACME protocol is secure and designed to be secure unencrypted, its important that the ACME protocol ONLY focuses on server security. Meaning that the server verfies the client in everything. The client never verifies the server as you can see in the
https://github.com/sebastiannielsen/acme-static
project - I can serve static data to a ACME client and it will happily accept it.
This is however a good thing (as seen in the acme-static project) but that means there must be additional protections against a "malicious ACME server". (attacker-controlled) - when it comes to DNS-PERSIST-01 since it relies solely on ACME-server-provided information.

This is why the security recommendation is only relevant for DNS-PERSIST-01 since that currently relies 100% on server-supplied information.

So I understand fully why the author of the document included that paragraph.
The problem is that the author incorrectly refers to issuer-domain-name, which is a opaque value that has zero meaning in the context.

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body: I am fine going with this change and I see why keeping the language makes sense. Requiring the pub key stuff to be mandatory is something that has been floated but I feel is much larger in scope than this paragraph change.

comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
@birgelee Now I replied to the question if it should be merged into main or rebased (I choose to merge into main) so now it should be all set to actually approve and merge completely when you want.

There is a discussion making key authorization mandatory for DNS-PERSIST-01 so might be better to wait until that is completed - and actually scrap the portion about DNSSEC and DNS Security if its changed so Key Authorization is always mandatory.

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body:
I understand mandatory key authorization is an ongoing discussion, but I think it is safe to move forward with this language change and if we go there we can remove the language in that push.

(FWIW I am against mandatory key authorization and I would like to keep the non-ACME options available so I think this is good language to have in there).

pulls.title: Replace the three accounturi modes with a single hashed account URI
pulls.author: birgelee
pulls.body:
Makes a client-computed hashed URI the sole `accounturi` form, replacing the three modes of -01: the raw ACME account URL (3a), alternative URIs (3b), and subscriber-account URIs (3c). This branch is the working candidate for -02.

The hashed URI is `<accountHashPrefix>/<hash-alg>/<base64url digest>`, where the digest is computed over `length_of_domain || domain_name || key || account_URL`. Binding the account key closes the substitution gap of a raw account URL: a record validates only for an account that controls the key, so a poisoned delivery channel cannot bind a record to an unintended account. Binding the domain gives each domain a distinct record value, which mitigates the correlation risk noted in RFC 8657, Section 5.9. A client that wants one record reused across domains can set `domain_name` to `*` and accept the correlation trade-off.

Changes:

1. Define the hashed-URI construction, with `sha-256` as the initial algorithm and agility through the `<hash-alg>` token.
2. Specify verification by CA-side recomputation, plus the key-retention rules that let records survive routine key rotation. Precedence: account deactivation overrides all retention, then certificate-backed retention, then general retention.
3. Add two directory `meta` fields with IANA registrations: `accountHashPrefix` (base URI for hashed values) and `keyRotationPeriod` (bound on prior-key acceptance).
4. Remove modes 3b and 3c and their dependent text: subscriber-compromise and broad-scope security considerations, DNS-spoofing amplification, mode-specific error handling, and the three-mode revocation table.
5. Rewrite the security considerations around the hashed URI: non-transferability, substitution resistance, enumeration cost, and the stated limits of the privacy protection.
6. Add a worked hashed-URI example that doubles as a test vector, including the domain-omitted `*` form, and update all record examples.
