comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
> moving towards a system where only 3b is allowed in the draft. I propose doing that in the next update.

In that case, I think support for omitting the domain should be added.

My suggestion is then that a client who wishes to opt out of privacy, then  sets domain_name to the wildcard character "*" (0x2a) before hashing.
This will allow a client to opt out of privacy, but still have full security by the other armaments.

A client may wish to provision the same record to multiple domains, or even synthesize using wildcard or use CNAME to point multiple domains to the same validation record.

Unless there's some ACME restriction I'm missing, domain names can actually contain NUL bytes. Domain labels (e.g. www, example and com) are represented in DNS as length + value and can contain any octet including dots, spaces and null bytes (DNS is also case insensitive).

Null bytes cannot appear in base64url encoded data or a URI so the last null byte does unambiguously mark the end of the domain name.

Edit: The key is not base64url encoded and so can contain null bytes. Maybe null bytes in domains should just be prohibited for this method.

> Unless there's some ACME restriction I'm missing

It's not an ACME restriction, but the normalization algorithm prescribed by this spec will fail if the domain name contains ASCII control characters. Specifically, ToASCII will fail as U+0000 is DISALLOWED by RFC 5892.

There's also the RFC 5280 requirement that dNSName GeneralNames be in "preferred name syntax", which would implicitly disallow NUL-containing hostnames to appear in the final certificate.

Given these, the ACME server should reject dns identifiers containing NULs.

In general I agree with @CBonnell that both the normalization and the guidance on "preferred name syntax" will both ensure that a domain containing a null byte would not make it this far into the processing (essentially the fact that the hashes are no longer unique is irrelevant as one could not practically get a certificate for this domain anyways via this method).

However, I do tend to prefer standards that are as self-contained as possible and don't rely on restrictions published in other documents. Given that in this encoding the length of the domain name cannot be more than 255 bytes, this single null byte terminator could just be replaced by a length byte leading the domain name. I will probably do that in a commit just to avoid confusion. From my perspective this change has a negligible impact on the implementation.

reviews.author: sheurich
reviews.body:
Reviewed the hashed-URI construction and the surrounding changes. The core is sound: `SHA-256(domain_name || 0x00 || key || account_URL)`, recomputed by the CA over the requesting account's key, restores RFC 8555 non-transferability for mode 3b. An attacker can't make an honest CA accept a victim's digest for the attacker's account without the victim's private key. The test vector checks out and the privacy framing is honest about being best-effort.

I have three blocking concerns and a set of smaller ones. The largest is that this adds a verifiable mode but leaves the default path (mode 3a, raw account URL) unbound, and deletes the text that documented that gap.

Separately, I've come around to Aaron's position: the binding should be mandatory for the default account path, and mode 3c should be cut from this draft. 3c can't carry the client-computed binding by construction, and the subscriber-account capability survives under BR method 3.2.2.4.22 and CP/CPS without being specified here. That's an authors' decision rather than a line comment, so I've raised it by mail; the inline comments below assume the current mode structure and flag where each item changes if we cut 3c.

Blocking:

1. Mode 3a is still `SHOULD accept` with no client-computed binding, so the substitution attack still succeeds against it, and this PR removes the "Substitution of the Account URI" subsection and the 3a self-check that documented it. We shouldn't ship the deletion without a replacement, whatever we decide on mandatory binding.
2. The revocation table keeps "Deactivate ACME account -> 3b immediate," but the normative text that backed it was removed and the prior-key retention rule would keep a deactivated account's records validating. Deactivation needs to override retention in normative text.
3. The key-retention requirement needs to be stated as an explicit CA data obligation (retain {account, key-thumbprint} plus the cert-to-validating-key link), with deactivation ranked above the MUST-not-prune rule.

Non-blocking: hard-coded SHA-256 with no agility signal; the "3b" label is silently redefined from the published -01 meaning (alternative URI), which is a real changelog hazard since -01 is public on the Datatracker; RFC 6234 is an Informational downref on a standards-track normative reference; and the one-to-one binding claim from the cover note should be stated in the text as the property RFC 8657 Section 5.4 actually needs (each hashed URI uniquely identifies one account, which holds under collision resistance because account_URL is a hash input). Details inline.

comments.body: Tighten this so it's unambiguous under wildcard/subdomain validation: the hash must bind the FQDN where the record is provisioned (the Validation Domain Name minus the `_validation-persist` label), not the requested certificate FQDN. "the FQDN being validated" invites the wrong reading. Binding the record's own domain is also what neutralizes the wildcard/CNAME uniqueness concern from #64 — worth stating as a positive property here.

The algorithm is fixed to SHA-256 with no agility path. The mitigating factor is real (the CA recomputes rather than a consumer parsing a prefix, unlike the old `pubkey:` proposal), so a CA could migrate by changing `accountHashPrefix` and the algorithm together. Either say that explicitly as the migration story, or add an algorithm identifier. This will come up in WG review given the history.

Two fixes here. First, typo: "that is know to the CA" -> "known." Second, the prior-key acceptance needs to be subordinate to account deactivation — as written, retention would keep a deactivated account's records validating. Add: "A CA MUST NOT accept a hashed URI computed from the keys of a deactivated account, regardless of retention." See the revocation-table comment.

State this as an explicit CA data-retention obligation, not just a pruning rule: the CA retains {account, key-thumbprint} associations and the link from a currently-valid certificate to the key that validated its backing record. And rank the rules: deactivation overrides the MUST-not-prune-while-cert-valid requirement, so a compromised-key deactivation stops validation immediately even if a valid cert depends on that key.

This PR removed the "Substitution of the Account URI" subsection that used to sit around here, and the challenge-object 3a self-check. Don't drop that content without a replacement: after this change, mode 3a's substitution weakness is both unmitigated and undocumented. At minimum, keep a subsection stating (a) mode 3b is the substitution-resistant path via key binding, and (b) raw mode 3a is a URL commitment only as good as the channel that delivered the account URL, and does not preserve RFC 8555 non-transferability when that URL was poisoned. (If we adopt mandatory binding on the default path, this changes accordingly, but we still need it.)

Two things for this security subsection. (1) Add a sentence closing Max's length-extension concern on the record: because the digest is compared for exact equality against a CA-recomputed value with fixed field structure, there's no attacker-controlled suffix to exploit, and `domain_name` as the leading field blocks cross-domain linkage. Bare SHA-256 is fine here; HMAC wouldn't help since both sides use only public inputs. (2) The one-to-one binding you describe in the cover note is worth stating precisely here: what RFC 8657 Section 5.4 requires is reverse-direction uniqueness — a URI must not identify two accounts — which holds because `account_URL` is a hash input and SHA-256 is collision resistant. Say "each hashed URI uniquely identifies one account" rather than "1-1 binding."

This "immediate" for 3b is currently unbacked — the normative text that enforced it was removed with the old mode-3b definition. Either restore an equivalent normative rule (see the deactivation comment on the mode-3b definition, line 181) or the table overstates what the spec guarantees. Related: if we cut 3c (see the review body and my mail to the authors), the row below and the 3c column come out entirely, which also resolves the deactivation-semantics gap for that mode — so let's settle the 3c question before reworking this table.

Changelog flag: -01 was published to the Datatracker with mode 3b meaning "alternative URI." This PR silently repurposes "3b" for the hashed URI. Add an explicit "mode 3b redefined" note in the document, or give the hashed URI a fresh label and retire the old 3b, so implementers tracking -01 aren't caught out. (Also: RFC 6234, cited normatively for SHA-256, is Informational — a downref the IESG will flag at Last Call. Cite FIPS 180-4 or be ready to note the downref.)
The URI classification is not in draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist-01. However this would be the first URI in the spec which isn't provided by the server so it might still be note worthy.

My concern wasn't with the use of wildcards, it was with the lack of separation between a domain and the ACME account URI which introduced ambiguity when using wildcards. The separator is what mitigates my concern.

I am still leaning towards going to a length byte at the beginning instead of the separator so the separation is clearly self contained and not dependent on the precondition that there are no null bytes in the domain name.

A length byte would also be effective in separating the domain from other fields, [RFC 1035 Section 2.3.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1035/#section-2.3.4) already limits domain names to 255 bytes.

I do not think we should use null character as terminating character. In some programming languages this character can be hard to produce.

If a termination character is needed, I would instead suggest a character which are prohibited in a domain, like the pipe character ( |, 0x7c ) - but still can be printed using a regular keyboard, and which is identical in both ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8.

The JWK thumbprint I think should be in base64url - not raw sha256 - most ACME tools already have functions that return a JWK thumbprint in base64url to append to key authorizations, so its benefical if these tools and functions can be reused.

Why mot base64url encoded? In this case, it would be preferable, since most ACME libraries already have functions for computing the keyAuthorization for HTTP-01 and DNS-01 authentication, which returns the JWK thumbprint in Base64url encoding.

I feel that base64url should be used here aswell so the same library and functions can be used also for DNS-PERSIST-01.

I am personally not that opinionated on this front. I felt it was strange to use a url-friendly encoding in what is a binary input and even if helper functions returned the base64url version it could just be decoded into raw bytes by whatever function was computing this hash.

That said I don't feel strongly about this. I am curious if other WG members have thoughts.
I agree with @sebastiannielsen that using base64url encoding of the thumbprint is easier to implement, because the base64url encoding of the thumbprint is used in other parts of the ACME spec.
This could require a registry for hash algorithms (if a suitable one doesn't already exist) with algorithm support status (e.g. MUST, RECOMMENDED, MAY, NOT RECOMMENDED, MUST NOT).

Is there a limit to the number of digests a CA would have to compute i.e. could an account have 200 keys that need to be checked?

It might make sense to either limit the number of concurrently valid keys for validation or have the client tell the ACME server which key is being used.
It might also be worth saying that capturing an http-01 challenge gives the JWK fingerprint of the ACME account which could be enough to perform a brute force attack to recover the account URI.

Its not possible to "capture" an http-01 challenge as that would require knowledge of the token.

Unless the server is configured to respond with a "minted" response based on any token input - but thats a conscious configuration by the server administrator, where the server administator is fully aware of its privacy implications. Its not possible to configure a server in that way by mistake.

HOWEVER, there is a risk when using dns-01 challenges since those are posted at a static location (_validation-persist.DOMAIN.TLD with no random input required), but you should not really mix dns-01 and dns-persist-01 - the server administrator should choose one. So thats a non-issue, if you have access to DNS, there is no reason to mix dns-01 and dns-persist-01, then you can aswell go with dns-persist-01 for everything.

Sorry if it wasn't clear, by capture I was referring to something passive on path to the CA.

This concern doesn't apply to dns-01 and tls-alpn-01 as they both use a digest of the key authorisation so the JWK thumbprint can't be recovered.

1: You can't do this to the ACME client, since the requests between the ACME client and server is encrypted. So even if server administrator sits on a unprotected wifi, it won't matter.

2: The path out from the CA (outgoing validationn requests, unencrypted in http-01) should be assumed to be protected. Its part of the CA's audit that their infrastructure is secure enough.

3: Only way to capture http-01 would then be if the SERVER in question sits on a unprotected wifi or wifi PTP link or if any part of the network on the server side is using hubs instead of switches. Very rare configuration.

4: This would then only have privacy implications, not any security implication.

My suggestion is that the CA should only save one previous key at maximum, and max period to save is 30 days. This makes it clear that if you want to do a key rollover, you have to create the new record.

1 month is enough even for those that don't have access to DNS but need to phone call their web host to have DNS changed,

I think we can do as same as with the ACME account keys - a CA *must* accept sha256, which is the "gold standard" but may accept more. For example, lets encrypt accept alg=ES384 even if thats not part of the standard and normally ES256 is used.

So a registry isn't needed, people coding clients will put in their own registrys in the software for which CAs support which algoritms.

JWK algorithm names and semantics are still tracked by an IANA registry https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-algorithms.

I couldn't find a similar registry listing hash algorithms and future algorithms could require different semantics e.g. a null algorithm that just base64 encodes the data.

Resolved in the direction @sebastiannielsen and @CBonnell describe: draft PR #68 redefines `key` as the 43-octet unpadded base64url RFC 7638 thumbprint, the same encoding ACME key authorizations already use (RFC 8555, Section 8.1), and recomputes both example vectors. The choice is cryptographically neutral and the field stays fixed length, so the deciding factor is that ACME libraries already produce this exact form.

The registry you are looking for exists: RFC 6920 established the IANA Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry for exactly this purpose. Draft PR #68 draws `<hash-alg>` from that registry's Hash Name Strings, makes `sha-256` mandatory to implement (the floor @sebastiannielsen describes), and restricts usable entries to non-truncated digests of at least 256 bits, which keeps out truncated variants and anything that is not a real digest. A managed namespace beats per-client tables of CA support: clients and CAs get algorithm agility without pairwise coordination, and each token's semantics stay pinned to its registry entry.

Right on the mechanism: HTTP-01 serves `token || "." || base64url(JWK_Thumbprint(accountKey))` over the CA's cleartext validation fetch, so an on-path observer can recover the thumbprint directly; dns-01 and tls-alpn-01 hash the key authorization instead. And agreed on the consequence: with the thumbprint in hand, an attacker can brute-force candidate account URLs offline, so account-URL entropy is the remaining barrier. Draft PR #68 adds exactly this caveat to the privacy analysis: the hashed URI offers best-effort resistance to bulk correlation, not strong unlinkability, and HTTP-01 use reduces the remaining protection to account-URL entropy.
Could the hash algorithm for the JWK thumbprint be the same as the overall hash algorithm e.g. if sha-384 is used to compute the account URI then it should be used for the JWK thumbprint as well.

I would keep the two algorithms independent. RFC 8555 Section 8.1 defines the ACME key-authorization thumbprint with SHA-256, and PR #68 deliberately reuses that exact 43-octet base64url value. Making the inner thumbprint follow `<hash-alg>` would define another thumbprint profile for every optional outer hash and prevent clients from reusing ACME's existing component. A stronger outer hash therefore does not remove the construction's SHA-256 dependency, but ACME key authorization has the same dependency. Replacing it should be a coordinated ACME change, not an implicit consequence of selecting a different outer hash.

pulls.title: Apply review fixes and issue resolutions (#38, #42, #56, #60)
pulls.author: sheurich
pulls.body:
Fixes against the -02 candidate (#67), reviewed at f816113. Both test vectors recomputed; build and lint clean.

Review fixes:

- Rewrite the stale Account Key Rotation text: the account URL is stable, but the hashed accounturi changes with the account key, so clients republish after rollover.
- Clarify that the CAA accounturi (the account URL, RFC 8657 Section 3.1) and the dns-persist accounturi (the hashed URI) are distinct values matched by different procedures.
- Document HTTP-01 thumbprint exposure as a privacy limit.

Construction changes from the #67 review threads:

- Hash the 43-octet unpadded base64url RFC 7638 thumbprint, the same form as the key-authorization component.
- Define hash-alg as an RFC 6920 Hash Name String; sha-256 mandatory for clients and CAs.

Issue resolutions:

- #38: clients check persistUntil against local provisioning state before starting an order.
- #42: DNS TTL no longer limits validation-data reuse; reuse is bounded by persistUntil and the CA's Validation Data Reuse Period.
- #56: the challenge-object member issuer-domain-names becomes issuerDomainNames; DNS parameter names are unchanged.
- #60: CAs must advertise issuerDomainNames in directory metadata, with the D ⊆ C consistency rule and the IANA registration. C ⊆ I applies only when caaIdentities is advertised.

Two additions go beyond what the issue threads literally agreed; let me know if you disagree:

- Optional hash algorithms must be 256-bit or longer, non-truncated registry entries (the RFC 6920 registry includes sha-256-32).
- persistUntil now also ends reuse of previously obtained validation data; the old record-format sentence contradicted the #42 direction.

Deliberately untouched: keyRotationPeriod and the domain-omitted * form; those will be follow-ups.

Refs #38, #42, #56, #60.

comments.author: MaxHearnden
comments.body:
> Optional hash algorithms must be 256-bit or longer, non-truncated registry entries (the RFC 6920 registry includes sha-256-32).

This will make sure that we're [SP 800-131A Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/131/a/r3/ipd) (currently a draft) compliant (migrating from 112 to 128 bits of security).

comments.author: birgelee
comments.body: I am all good on merging this. One one comment is on the new proposal to have DNS persist records break on ACME key change. I know the records are computed over the key, but I think there is a strong security justification for why they don't need to break on key rollover. I will probably chat more about this coming up. I like to keep everything moving so I would rather merge this in and then change the behavior if we decide to go there.

comments.author: sebastiannielsen
comments.body:
> I am all good on merging this. One one comment is on the new proposal to have DNS persist records break on ACME key change.

I feel that if someone wants to do key rollover, they should also replace the record. Keeping a old record indefinitely creates security risks, especially if a key is moved from an account to another - which creates ambigiutiy, especially if 2 CAs share infrastructure, have different caaIdentities, but identical accounturi's and account databases.

(the requirement for 2 different CAs to have distinct account uri's only applies if they also share caaIdentities).

The prescribed keyRotationPeriod meta record allows a client to do a emergency key rotation, and then do the record replacement.

Which can be done like how DNSSEC key rotation is made - publish the new record, wait until it goes live in all DNS caches, and only after then, delete the old record.

I don't see a need for supporting infinitely old records just to allow key rotation with no access to DNS at all, which increases storage space and requirements for CA's. Its enough they need to retain all deactivated accounts, having to retain all keys - especially now when ML-DSA is waiting behind the door will create problems, especially if a client does multiple key rotations.

Requiring CAA for this method could pose a risk for organisations using private CAs as the organisation could have to publish additional CAA records where the CAA identity is not protected from reuse by another CA.

This might be better suited for the CA/B Forum TLS baseline requirements.

Using the Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry might mean that we should use one of the formats defined by RFC 6920 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6920), in particular we could use the URL segment format (e.g. sha-256;UyaQV-Ev4rdLoHyJJWCi11OHfrYv9E1aGQAlMO2X_-Q) or the .well-known URL format (e.g. http://example.com/.well-known/ni/sha-256/UyaQV-Ev4rdLoHyJJWCi11OHfrYv9E1aGQAlMO2X_-Q).

Fair catch. Two fixes coming out of this.

The intent of C ⊆ I is a single identity vocabulary: the name in a domain's CAA policy and in its `_validation-persist` record should be the same string for the same CA. That only makes sense where the CA participates in CAA validation, so the fix is scoping rather than dropping: the blanket "MUST advertise `caaIdentities`" is removed and the rule becomes conditional. If the CA advertises `caaIdentities`, every value in C MUST also appear there. A CA that doesn't do CAA validation never touches the CAA identity namespace, and a new sentence notes the identity-reuse caveat for CAs outside the CCADB/BR disclosure regime.

Your comment also surfaced an adjacent bug: as written, a missing `caaIdentities` array knocked out pre-provisioning entirely. That should only depend on `issuerDomainNames`; fixed in the same commit.

For publicly trusted CAs the mandate has audit teeth in the BRs rather than in this document; that side belongs with the CABF Method 3.2.2.4.22 cleanup work (cabforum/servercert#674-#677 territory).

Fixed in 5680afd.

The narrow reuse is intentional: this draft uses the RFC 6920 Hash Name String registry, not the RFC 6920 name formats. The value here identifies an ACME account under the CA's `accountHashPrefix`; it does not name retrievable content whose bytes are checked against the digest. Requiring an `ni:` URI or the `/.well-known/ni/` HTTP mapping would import content-naming and dereferencing semantics this value does not have, and it would constrain the CA's URI layout. The draft therefore does not adopt or depend on either format.
